name: What Is a Qubit
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Beyond the Bit: What a Qubit Actually Is
lesson.summary: Introduces the qubit as the two-level quantum system that generalizes the classical bit, covering its mathematical description, physical realizations, and the Bloch sphere picture.
lesson.body:
Every digital device you have ever used, from a phone to a supercomputer, stores and processes information in bits. A classical bit is beautifully simple: at any instant it is either 0 or 1, represented physically by a voltage being high or low, a transistor being on or off, or a small region of a disk being magnetized one way or the other. This strict either/or nature is what makes classical computing so reliable. Once you read a bit, you get a definite answer, and reading it again gives you the same answer.

A qubit, short for quantum bit, is the quantum mechanical generalization of this idea. Like a classical bit, a qubit has two distinguishable basis states, written in physics notation as |0⟩ and |1⟩ (read "ket zero" and "ket one"). But unlike a classical bit, a qubit is not restricted to being purely in one of those two states. Quantum mechanics allows it to exist in a combination of both at once, described mathematically as a vector alpha|0⟩ + beta|1⟩, where alpha and beta are complex numbers called probability amplitudes, and the squared magnitude of each amplitude gives the probability of finding the qubit in that state when it is measured. What that combination means physically, rather than just mathematically, is the subject of the next section on superposition.

Physically, a qubit can be built from any system with two well defined quantum states that can be controlled and measured. Superconducting circuits, cooled to a fraction of a degree above absolute zero, use two distinct energy levels of a tiny artificial atom etched onto a chip. Trapped ion quantum computers use two electronic energy levels of a single charged atom held in place by electromagnetic fields. Photonic approaches use a property like the polarization of a single photon, horizontal versus vertical. These platforms differ enormously in engineering detail, but each is trying to isolate and control the same underlying mathematical object: a two level quantum system.

A standard way to visualize a single qubit's state is the Bloch sphere. Picture a globe where the north pole represents |0⟩ and the south pole represents |1⟩. A classical bit could only ever sit at one of those two poles. A qubit's state, by contrast, can correspond to any point on the surface of that sphere. This is a visualization tool for the mathematics of a single qubit, not a claim that some tiny object is literally spinning around inside a ball, but it captures something real: a qubit's description carries more information than a simple on or off switch, even though, as later sections will show, any single measurement of it still only ever returns one of two classical outcomes.

That last point matters because it is the seed of everything that follows in this book. A single qubit by itself does not let you compute anything a classical bit cannot, since one measurement collapses it to a plain 0 or 1. The real power of quantum computing comes from combining many qubits so that their possible joint states, and the way those states can become correlated with one another, grow far faster than any classical system's could. Understanding precisely what a qubit is, as a mathematical and physical object, is the prerequisite for understanding why groups of them behave in ways that have no classical analogue at all.
